routes.label: Prove a lower bound and build a wall attaining it

question:
A block wall \(100\) feet long and \(7\) feet high will be constructed using blocks that are \(1\) foot high and either \(2\) feet long or \(1\) foot long (no blocks may be cut). The vertical joins in the blocks must be staggered as shown, and the wall must be even on the ends. What is the smallest number of blocks needed to build this wall?

[Figure 1](figures/2000_AMC_8_Q12_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The wall has seven rows because each block is \(1\) foot high. To prove a smallest number, we need both a lower bound and an arrangement that reaches it.

Each \(100\)-foot row needs at least \(100\div2=50\) blocks, since no block is longer than \(2\) feet. A row with exactly \(50\) blocks must use only \(2\)-foot blocks. Its internal joins are then \(2,4,6,\ldots,98\) feet from the left end. Consequently, two adjacent rows cannot both have exactly \(50\) blocks, because their joins would line up.

Number the rows from bottom to top. Each of the three separate pairs \((1,2)\), \((3,4)\), and \((5,6)\) therefore needs at least \(50+51=101\) blocks. Row \(7\) needs at least \(50\). These groups include every row exactly once, so every allowed wall needs at least
\[
3\cdot101+50=353
\]
blocks.

We can attain this bound. Use \(50\) two-foot blocks in each of rows \(1,3,5,7\). In each of rows \(2,4,6\), place a one-foot block at each end with \(49\) two-foot blocks between them. Each such row has length \(1+49\cdot2+1=100\) feet and uses \(51\) blocks. Its joins are at \(1,3,5,\ldots,99\) feet, so none lines up with a join in an adjacent row. Both ends of the wall are even.

This construction uses
\[
4\cdot50+3\cdot51=\boxed{353}
\]
blocks, proving that the minimum is \(353\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
